title: Be still (Psalm 45 [46])
hookLine: mountains fall into the sea, and God says be still and see that I am God
last: WHY ART THOU SAD, MY SOUL?

lines: A MUG WITH A CALM LAKE.
cards: The words turn up on mugs and wall prints, in soft script over a calm lake: be still. It looks like a spa slogan. Breathe.
Relax. Light a candle. But go back to where the line comes from, and there's no calm lake anywhere.
The ground is shaking. Mountains are sliding into the ocean. The sea is roaring.
Nations are at war. And right in the middle of all that noise, God speaks.

teach.b: Psalm 45 in the Douay, 46 in most Bibles, opens: "Our God is our refuge and strength: a helper in troubles, which have found us exceedingly." Troubles that found us, as if they came looking.
Then the disaster: "Therefore we will not fear, when the earth shall be troubled; and the mountains shall be removed into the heart of the sea." The solid ground itself gives way.
And in the middle of the chaos, a quiet picture: "The stream of the river maketh the city of God joyful." Jerusalem had no great river.

teach.h: A RIVER MAKES THE CITY GLAD.
teach.b: The psalm gives it one anyway, a gentle stream that makes a city glad while the sea rages. Then God speaks. He makes wars cease to the ends of the earth, breaks the bow, burns the shields.
And then: "Be still and see that I am God." Here's the surprise.

teach.h: BE STILL: LET GO, DROP YOUR HANDS.
teach.b: The Hebrew word behind be still is usually rendered let go: relax your grip, stop. It's less a spa word than a word you'd shout at two armies: enough, put it down.
The Latin Bible put it as vacate: be free, make room. So the line is a command to stop fighting, stop grasping, stop trying to hold the mountains up yourself, and see who God is.
In this psalm, stillness isn't what you do once life is calm. It's what you do while it isn't.

how: Catholics pray Psalm 45 [46] in the Liturgy of the Hours and hear it at Mass, including on the feast of the Dedication of the Lateran Basilica, where the river that makes the city of God glad is read alongside images of the Temple.

o: freeze in place so no one notices you
stay calm and relaxed, like a quiet lake
let go: stop fighting and drop your hands

games.q: what's inside the psalm — tap the pairs.
p: removed into the heart of the sea
makes the city of God joyful
the Latin: be free, make room

s: be still first appears in a psalm about a calm lake
it comes in the middle of earthquakes, a roaring sea and war.
the Hebrew for be still is close to let go or drop your hands
less relax, more stop fighting and put it down.
the psalm gives the city of God a river
the stream of the river maketh the city of God joyful.

games.q: the ground is shaking, the sea is roaring and armies are fighting. what does God say in the psalm?
o: be still, and see that I am God.
games.why: he breaks the bow and burns the shields, and then says: be still and see that I am God. a command to stop, not a mood.

practice: For sixty seconds, be still, not calm, just still: let your hands drop into your lap, palms open, as if you've just put something heavy down.
Notice what's shaking in your life right now; you don't have to fix any of it for this minute, just stop holding it up.
If you pray, hear the line as God's word to you, be still and see that I am God; if you don't, simply let your hands stay open.

wordCard.voice: Be still. In the psalm, not a spa word but a command in the middle of chaos: let go, drop your hands, and see. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: let go, relax your grip, stop. translated be still.

carryVoice: Your line: be still and see. The mountains were never yours to hold up. Day one hundred seventy, done.
